description:
Found by measuring the goal program's allocations, which is what the epic's
SIGNAL asks for.

    case bin do
      <<s :: binary-size(n), rest :: binary>> -> {:ok, s, rest}
      _ -> :error
    end

    take("hello world", 5)
      elixir  {:ok, "hello", " world"}
      fz      :error          on every door, silently

A LITERAL size works -- `binary-size(5)` on the same input returns
`{:ok, "hello", " world"}` -- so it is specifically a bound variable as the
size. No error, no warning: the clause just never fires.

WHY IT IS P1 RATHER THAN A CURIOSITY. Without it, no library function can take
a SLICE of a binary whose length it computed. Every string-building routine has
to accumulate one byte at a time:

    fnp string(<<c, r :: binary>>, acc), do: string(r, acc <> <<c>>)

which allocates a new binary per byte. Measured on the goal program, decoding a
68-byte JSON document costs 435 BITSTRING ALLOCATIONS and 71,600 bytes. The
document's string content is about ten bytes. That is O(n^2) in the length of
every string, and it is the exact shape this epic exists to remove -- "the
compiler is ahead of the library; the library squanders it".

With variable sizes working, a scanner finds the extent and takes ONE slice:
435 allocations become a handful.

DONE = a bound variable as a binary segment's size matches the bytes it names,
on all three doors, with a fixture. Then re-measure the JSON allocation golden;
the drop is the point.

WATCH OUT: `BitSize::Var` exists in the AST, so the surface parses it and
something downstream drops or misreads it. Whatever that is, a size the matcher
cannot honour should be a diagnostic, not a clause that never fires -- the same
lesson as fz-5xp.52.

comments.text:
DIAGNOSED, and narrower than it first looked.

The DISPATCH path is broken; plain DESTRUCTURING works:

    fnp take(bin, n) do
      <<s :: binary-size(n), rest :: binary>> = bin      # works
      {:ok, s, rest}
    end

    case bin do
      <<s :: binary-size(n), rest :: binary>> -> ...      # never matches
    end

Destructuring goes through `lower_bitstring_pattern`, whose
`LoweredBitSize::Value` carries a ValueId the interpreter resolves from the
environment (`backend_bit_size_value`). That is correct today.

Clause heads and `case` go through the DISPATCH MATRIX instead, and the plan
resolves a size name only against bindings the PATTERN ITSELF makes:

  * dispatch_matrix/pattern.rs looks the name up in `binding_subjects`, which
    holds names bound by EARLIER FIELDS of the same bitstring, and otherwise
    emits `BitstringFieldSize::BindingName(name)`;
  * ir_interp/dispatch_exec.rs resolves `BindingName` from
    `state.direct_bindings` -- again, the pattern's own bindings.

So `<<a, s :: binary-size(a)>>` (size bound by an earlier field) works, and a
size from the ENCLOSING SCOPE -- a function parameter, or anything bound before
the `case` -- is never found. The size comes back absent and the clause fails
silently.

THE SHAPE OF THE FIX. An outer-scope name in a pattern already has a mechanism:
pinning. `Pattern::Pinned` reaches dispatch through a `pinned` map
(`load_pinned_dispatch_value`). An unbound size name should resolve the same
way rather than through `direct_bindings`. Four consumers to keep in step:
canon.rs, native_codegen/receive.rs, jobs/native.rs and ir_interp/dispatch_exec.rs.

WORKAROUND until then: destructure, do not match. That is enough to fix the JSON
scanner's O(n^2) string building.

PARTIAL landed: the interpreter now refuses instead of silently mismatching, so
all three doors agree that this form is unsupported. Full support -- resolving an
outer-scope size through the pin mechanism -- remains, with the design in the
earlier comment. Ticket stays open for that.

title: [BUG] A variable-size binary segment silently never matches
